title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether deterministic verifier augmentation (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation = 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, calibrated adversarial injection, and exploratory ROC estimation) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived (execution/*, analysis/*).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operator productivity gains for network operations (NetOps) but raises safety risks: an incorrect or ill‑timed change can break reachability, violate policy, or cause outages. Prior work therefore promotes tool‑grounding and generate–validate–repair pipelines to reduce constraint violations and hallucination‑driven errors. To produce replicable evidence about such pipelines, we preregistered a workflow‑centred, paired experiment that compares an LLM baseline to a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on synthetic NetOps tasks. The primary research question (preregistered in cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) was: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) change the rate of unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts?

This paper (1) publishes the complete preregistered confirmatory run and deterministic artifacts; (2) presents an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory test was non‑informative in this execution; and (3) gives concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for designing informative repeats. We emphasize reproducibility: the analysis and accounting reported below come directly from archived artifacts (execution/model_configuration.json, execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg).
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and prototype reports document LLM applications to NetOps (intent translation, configuration synthesis, remediation) and propose architectures that augment LLMs with deterministic tools and verifiers to improve correctness [arXiv:2605.12729; SSRN:7132138; IEEE OJCOMS 2026]. Generate–validate–repair and divide–verify–refine pipelines reduce constraint violations in experimental settings, but demonstrated effect sizes depend on verifier fidelity, generation semantics, and prompt design [openalex:W4412888330; openalex:W7161354925]. Guardrail and red‑teaming literature stress trade‑offs between false refusals and unblocked unsafe proposals, and recommend replayable, sandboxed evaluations with archived scoring traces [TechRxiv:177004277; TechRxiv:177006109]. Our work complements these contributions by providing a fully preregistered, deterministic artifact bundle and a reproducible example of how execution semantics (shared vs independent generation) and budgeting choices interact with paired estimands and testability.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (SAFE encoded as 1). Design: paired binary comparison with N=200 unique tasks paired across two pipelines; primary test = exact McNemar two‑sided implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10000 resamples (seed = 1729).

Task generator and sampling. A deterministic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks using a preregistered RNG schedule (seed sequence beginning with seed = 42; per‑task generator seeds 1..200). Tasks targeted operationally meaningful changes limited to admin/mtu/vlan fields across multi‑device single‑AS topologies. The sampling split tasks into benign and adversarial clusters; adversarial prompts followed preregistered templated obfuscation/negation transforms intended to increase baseline unsafe rate. Task manifest and sample task entries are archived at execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Pipelines, validators, and scoring. Two pipelines were compared: baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (LLM candidate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional single repair). deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in a sandbox and applied full_intent_constraint_validation; scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) contain parsed command counts, violation lists, and validation_before/after traces used to encode binary outcomes (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). For the confirmatory episodes no automatic repairs were applied (repair_provider_trace = null in scoring JSONs), so the guarded arm's outcome depended on the validator verdict applied to the candidate.

Generation semantics and budget (critical preregistered choice). The preregistration explicitly allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (two LLM calls per pair) or shared_initial_candidate (one shared LLM call per pair). Independent per‑arm generation creates the per‑pair variability necessary to produce discordant outcomes (n10 or n01) that McNemar‑style inference requires. The executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false) and therefore performed exactly one LLM generation per pair; this is recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json. The preregistered maximum_model_calls for independent generation was 400; the executed shared scheme consumed model_calls_used = 200.

Analysis and missingness. The primary analysis was deterministic and executed by paired_binary_analysis_v1. Each pair produced two binary labels from the deterministic validator and the analysis produced the 2×2 contingency (n11, n10, n01, n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples; seed = 1729). Preregistered missingness handling allowed one retry for failed model calls and automatic replacement for contaminated tasks; no technical failures or replacements occurred and complete_pair_count = 200 (see analysis/missingness_summary.csv and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run completed planned_episode_count = 400 (200 paired tasks × 2 arm scorings derived from a single shared initial generation per task) with failed_episode_count = 0 and model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json; execution/model_configuration.json records independent_condition_generation = false). Provider call audit in deterministic_reconciliation.json shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and a single stage 'shared_initial_generation' per pair.

Primary outcomes. The archived analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline SAFE = 200/200 and guarded SAFE = 200/200 (SAFE encoded as 1). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). These numeric outputs are taken verbatim from analysis/results.json and the CSV artifacts.

Representative artifacts and diagnostics. Scoring JSON examples (execution/scoring/task-000001‑baseline.json and task-000001‑guarded.json; task‑000002 and task‑000003 examples archived) show identical shared_initial_candidate content across arms and validator traces with violation_count = 0 and valid = true in validation_before and validation_after. No repair_provider_trace entries are present for confirmatory episodes, confirming that the guarded pipeline did not change candidates in the confirmatory data. analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg provides the bar visualization archived with the numeric outputs.

Interpretation of numeric result. The absence of any discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0) is a ceiling/testability outcome: when the same LLM candidate is SAFE under the deterministic validator, neither arm can be UNSAFE without an applied repair that changes the candidate. In our confirmatory episodes no repairs were applied; therefore the paired contrast provides no information about whether the verifier could reduce unsafe proposals under conditions where the baseline is nonzero. The observed p = 1.0 and CI collapsed to a point reflect this lack of information, not evidence of verifier ineffectiveness.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded diagnosis of non‑informative confirmatory test. Three archived facts combined to make the preregistered estimand untestable in this run: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics were executed (execution/model_configuration.json; independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair LLM outputs reused across both arms (execution/responses/*‑shared‑initial.txt); (2) the sampled tasks and the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) yielded zero baseline unsafe proposals as validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (baseline SAFE = 200/200; analysis/condition_summary.csv); and (3) the execution budget choice (single shared generation) reduced model_calls_used to 200 rather than the preregistered 400 that independent per‑arm draws would have required (execution/execution_manifest.json). When a shared candidate is SAFE, and no repair modifies it, both arms must be concordant (n11), producing the observed ceiling.

Practical, artifact‑supported recommendations for informative repeats. These recommendations derive directly from the preregistration and the execution accounting artifacts and are implementable without inventing new tools:

1) Use independent per‑arm generation for paired causal contrasts. For N=200 pairs, independent draws require ≈200 additional LLM calls (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 vs executed 200). Archive the exact model call budget and enforce it at execution start.

2) Calibrate adversarial injection to create a nonzero baseline unsafe rate. The preregistered power plan targeted baseline unsafe ≈10–15%. Prior to confirmatory testing, use the preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) to tune adversarial transforms until baseline unsafe rates align with power assumptions; these exploratory runs should be archived and summarized (analysis artifacts reserved for exploratory ROC estimation).

3) Reserve and run an exploratory ROC procedure. Use the exploratory sample to estimate verifier true/false positive rates (verifier ROC) and refusal rates; archive validation traces for each exploratory item to permit deterministic reanalysis.

4) Make model‑call accounting explicit in preregistration. Record planned vs executed model_calls_used in the manifest and report it alongside inferential outputs to make budget–estimand trade‑offs transparent (execution/execution_manifest.json).

5) If budget constrained, prioritize independent per‑arm draws over broad multi‑model sampling because paired contrasts require per‑arm variability for statistical identification.

Evidence‑to‑claim mapping (concise). Principal empirical claims and their supporting archived artifacts: (A) observed per‑arm SAFE counts → analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; (B) shared generation semantics and model call accounting → execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json; (C) representative validator traces showing valid = true → execution/scoring/task‑00000X‑*.json; (D) analysis outputs (p‑value, CI) → analysis/results.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv. These artifact paths permit exact replay and verification of the numerical claims in this manuscript.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing a baseline LLM and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on N=200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The scientific contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑oriented: (1) we publish a complete preregistered run with deterministic artifacts enabling exact replay (execution/*, analysis/*); (2) we provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why the confirmatory test was non‑informative; and (3) we provide concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial budgeting, exploratory ROC estimation, and explicit model‑call accounting) to design informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle to support deterministic replays and community replication.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
